title: What the Bible Is
summary: A library of sixty-six books in two testaments and three languages: what is in it, how it is arranged, how Jewish, Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox Bibles differ, and what the Bible claims to be.

sections.h: A library, not a single book
sections.body:
The word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, ‘the books’, a plural. Biblion meant a scroll or written document, and the word itself goes back to Byblos, the Phoenician port through which papyrus, the paper of the ancient world, was traded into Greece. By the Middle Ages Latin speakers were treating biblia as a singular noun, and so ‘the books’ became ‘the Book’. Both names are true. The Bible is one book in the sense that the church has always received it as a single witness to one God and one story. It is also a library, and a reader who forgets this will be puzzled on almost every page.

The Protestant Bible, the one most English readers hold, contains sixty-six books: thirty-nine in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New. They were written over more than a thousand years, from the time of Israel's early kings (and, on traditional reckoning, earlier) to the end of the first century AD. Their writers include kings, priests, prophets, court officials, a tax collector, a physician, fishermen, and a former Pharisee; many books name no author at all. They were written in palaces and in exile, in prison cells and on the road, for audiences as different as a royal court in Jerusalem and a house church in Rome.

The library holds many kinds of writing. There is narrative (Genesis, Samuel, the Gospels, Acts), law (much of Exodus through Deuteronomy), poetry and song (Psalms, Song of Solomon, Lamentations), proverbs and wisdom argument (Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes), prophetic oracles (Isaiah through Malachi), letters (Romans through Jude), and apocalyptic vision (parts of Daniel, and Revelation). Each kind works by its own rules, as a newspaper, a hymnbook, a legal code, and a family letter do today. Much misreading of the Bible comes from reading one kind of writing as if it were another, a proverb as if it were a promise, a poem as if it were a lab report, or a vision as if it were a newspaper. The guides in the section on reading each kind of writing take these one at a time.

For all that variety, the books are not a random anthology. Later writers quote, echo, and answer earlier ones constantly. The prophets appeal to the covenant made at Sinai; the psalms retell the exodus; the New Testament writers quote the Old on nearly every page and claim that its story reaches its goal in Jesus of Nazareth. Luke opens his Gospel by explaining that he has investigated carefully so that his reader may have confidence: “so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:4). The Bible is a library that knows it is a library, and that reads itself.

The two great divisions of the Christian Bible are called the Old Testament and the New Testament. Testament here does not mean a will, or not only that. It comes from the Latin testamentum, which early Latin translators used for the Greek diathēkē, which in turn is the Greek Bible's word for the Hebrew berit, ‘covenant’. A covenant is a binding relationship between parties, sealed by oath, with promises and obligations on both sides; it is one of the Bible's central ideas. The name New Testament goes back to Jeremiah's promise that God would make a new covenant with Israel and Judah, writing his law on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:31-34), a promise Jesus claimed at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20) and the Letter to the Hebrews quotes at length (Hebrews 8:8-12). So the two parts of the Christian Bible are, in effect, the books of the old covenant and the books of the new.

Old does not mean obsolete. For the first Christians, the only Scriptures they had were the books of Israel; when Paul says that Christ died and rose “according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4), he means what Christians now call the Old Testament. The church has always read the two testaments together: the Old as the story and promise that the New assumes, and the New as the fulfillment that sends the reader back to the Old with new eyes. In the second century a teacher named Marcion tried to cut the Old Testament out entirely, along with the parts of the New that seemed too Jewish to him; the church rejected him, and that rejection has held ever since.

Jewish readers do not call their Scriptures the Old Testament, since for Judaism there is no New. The usual Jewish name is Tanakh, an acronym formed from the first letters of its three parts (Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim), or simply Mikra, ‘that which is read’. Many scholars use the neutral term Hebrew Bible. This Study Bible uses Old Testament when speaking within the Christian reading of the whole Bible and Hebrew Bible when describing the Jewish collection or the Hebrew text itself.

The Bible was written in three languages. Almost all of the Old Testament is in Hebrew, the language of ancient Israel, a Semitic language written from right to left in an alphabet of twenty-two consonants. For most of its history written Hebrew had no vowels; readers supplied them from knowledge of the language, and the vowel signs in printed Hebrew Bibles were added by the Masoretes, Jewish scholars of the early Middle Ages (see How We Got the Old Testament).

A small part of the Old Testament is in Aramaic, a related Semitic language that became the common tongue of the Near East under the Assyrian, Babylonian, and Persian empires. The Aramaic passages are Daniel 2:4b through 7:28, Ezra 4:8 through 6:18 and 7:12-26, one verse of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 10:11), and two words in Genesis 31:47, the Aramaic name Laban gives to a heap of witness stones. The Ezra passages are mostly official correspondence with the Persian court, quoted in the language the empire used for its business. By the time of Jesus, Aramaic was the everyday language of Jews in Galilee and Judea, and the Gospels preserve some of his Aramaic words: talitha koum, ‘little girl, get up’ (Mark 5:41), and ephphatha, ‘be opened’ (Mark 7:34).

The New Testament is written entirely in Greek, not the classical Greek of Plato but Koine, ‘common’ Greek, the international language spread through the eastern Mediterranean after Alexander the Great's conquests in the 330s and 320s BC. Koine was the language of trade, administration, and ordinary letters, which is why the New Testament could travel so quickly from Jerusalem to Antioch, Corinth, and Rome. Its writers also knew the Old Testament in a Greek translation, the Septuagint, made by Jews in Egypt in the last three centuries BC, and they often quote it. The style of the New Testament ranges from the plain Greek of Mark and Revelation to the polished periods of Luke's prologue and the Letter to the Hebrews.

No one needs these languages to read the Bible with understanding; translation is part of the Bible's own history, since the New Testament itself translates Jesus' Aramaic into Greek. But the languages explain a great deal that puzzles English readers: why a Hebrew poem repeats itself, why a verse number differs from one Bible to another, why a footnote says ‘Or’ and gives a second rendering. The Study Bible's notes explain the original words where they matter.

sections.h: How the Old Testament is arranged
sections.body:
Open a Hebrew Bible and a Christian Old Testament side by side and you will find the same books in a different order, and even a different count. The Jewish arrangement has three parts. The Torah (‘instruction’ or ‘law’) is the five books of Moses, Genesis through Deuteronomy. The Nevi'im (‘Prophets’) come in two groups: the Former Prophets, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings, which Christians call historical books but which Jewish tradition regards as prophetic history; and the Latter Prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve (Hosea through Malachi, counted as one book because they fit on a single scroll). The Ketuvim (‘Writings’) gather everything else: Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five short scrolls read at the festivals (Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther), Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah, and Chronicles. Because Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra-Nehemiah, and the Twelve each count as one, the Hebrew Bible numbers twenty-four books, though it contains exactly the same text as the Protestant thirty-nine. Jesus appears to refer to this threefold shape when he speaks of what is written about him “in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44), the Psalms standing at the head of the Writings.

The Christian order follows, broadly, the order of the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate. It groups the books by kind: five books of law, then the historical books from Joshua to Esther, then the poetic and wisdom books from Job to the Song of Solomon, then the prophets, with the four long books (Isaiah, Jeremiah with Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel) before the twelve short ones. Daniel moves from the Writings to the Prophets, and Ruth is placed after Judges because its story is set ‘in the days when the judges ruled’.

The two orders tell the story with different endings. The Hebrew Bible closes with Chronicles, whose last verse is Cyrus of Persia's decree inviting the exiles to go up and rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem, so that the canon ends on the road home. The Christian Old Testament closes with Malachi, whose last words promise that Elijah will come before the great day of the LORD, so that the Old Testament ends looking forward, and the next page is the Gospel of Matthew, where John the Baptist appears in the wilderness in the spirit of Elijah. Neither order is original in the sense of being written into the books themselves; both are ancient ways of reading the collection as a whole.

sections.h: How the New Testament is arranged
sections.body:
The New Testament's twenty-seven books fall into four groups. First come the four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, each a portrait of the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. The word gospel translates the Greek euangelion, ‘good news’, a word used in the Roman world for announcements such as a victory or the birth of an heir. The first three Gospels share much material and are called the Synoptic Gospels (from a Greek word for ‘seeing together’); John tells the story differently. The order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John is ancient but not chronological; most scholars think Mark was written first, though a minority, following the early church's tradition, hold that Matthew was.

Second comes Acts, Luke's second volume, which follows the apostles from Jerusalem to Rome over roughly thirty years. Third come the letters. Paul's thirteen letters are placed first and arranged, with one exception, by length within two groups: letters to churches (Romans, the longest, down to 2 Thessalonians) and then letters to individuals (1 Timothy down to Philemon, the shortest). They are not in the order Paul wrote them; 1 Thessalonians or Galatians is probably the earliest. After Paul come Hebrews, whose author is not named, and the seven general or catholic letters, so called because most are addressed to the church at large rather than to one congregation: James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2, and 3 John, and Jude. Last stands Revelation, a prophetic vision given to a man named John on the island of Patmos, which draws on the whole Old Testament to show the end of the story.

This order became standard in the Latin West; some ancient Greek manuscripts place the general letters immediately after Acts and before Paul, and the Letter to the Hebrews sometimes stands in the middle of Paul's letters, after 2 Thessalonians. Luther's German New Testament of 1522 moved Hebrews, James, Jude, and Revelation to the end because he doubted their standing, and German Lutheran Bibles long kept that order. The shape is a matter of arrangement, not of content, but it shapes reading: the Gospels come first because everything else depends on them.

sections.h: Jewish, Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox Bibles
sections.body:
All Christians share the same twenty-seven books of the New Testament. They differ over the Old Testament, and the difference lies in a group of Jewish writings from roughly the last three centuries before Christ that survive mainly in Greek and were included in the Septuagint. Protestants call these books the Apocrypha (‘hidden’ books); Catholics call them the deuterocanonical books (‘of the second canon’, meaning received later, not less inspired). The story of how the lists came to differ is told in How the Books Were Chosen; here is what the difference looks like on the shelf.

The Jewish Bible contains twenty-four books, identical in content to the Protestant Old Testament. The Protestant Bible has thirty-nine Old Testament books and sixty-six in all. The Reformers of the sixteenth century followed the Hebrew canon, which Jerome had also favored in the late fourth century; many early Protestant Bibles, including Luther's of 1534 and the King James Version of 1611, printed the Apocrypha in a separate section between the testaments, to be read for instruction but not used to establish doctrine. Most Protestant Bibles since the nineteenth century omit them.

The Catholic Bible has forty-six Old Testament books and seventy-three in all: the thirty-nine plus Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom (the Wisdom of Solomon), Sirach (also called Ecclesiasticus), and Baruch, whose sixth chapter is the Letter of Jeremiah. It also includes longer forms of Esther and Daniel, with Greek additions: in Daniel, the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three Young Men inserted in chapter 3, and the stories of Susanna (chapter 13) and Bel and the Dragon (chapter 14). The Council of Trent defined this list on 8 April 1546.

The Eastern Orthodox churches read the Old Testament from the Septuagint and accept the Catholic deuterocanonical books together with several more: 1 Esdras (called 2 Esdras or Esdras A in some Orthodox Bibles), 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, and Psalm 151, with 4 Maccabees often printed as an appendix. Orthodox usage is less tightly defined by council than Catholic; the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 affirmed the deuterocanonical books. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has the largest canon, usually counted as eighty-one books, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees, which survive complete only in Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia.

These differences are real, but they should be kept in proportion. Every Christian tradition receives the same Law, Prophets, Psalms, Gospels, and apostolic letters, and every tradition confesses the same creeds drawn from them. The disputed books do not carry any doctrine of the creeds, and Protestant scholars read them as valuable history and piety (1 Maccabees is a principal source for the Maccabean revolt behind the feast of Hanukkah, which John 10:22 calls the Feast of Dedication).

sections.h: What the Bible says about itself
sections.body:
The Bible does not contain a table of contents for itself, but its writers speak often about the word of God and about writing. The prophets introduce their messages with the formula ‘thus says the LORD’. Moses writes the words of the law in a book and has it placed beside the ark of the covenant (Deuteronomy 31:24-26). Jeremiah's scroll, burned by King Jehoiakim, is dictated again to Baruch the scribe (Jeremiah 36). Isaiah sets the permanence of God's word against the frailty of everything human: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Paul says that Israel was “entrusted with the very words of God” (Romans 3:2).

Two New Testament passages have shaped the church's teaching most directly. In 2 Timothy 3:16, Paul writes: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness”. The word translated God-breathed, theopneustos, appears only here; it says that Scripture comes out of God as breath comes from a mouth, and it is the root of the doctrine of inspiration. In context Paul is speaking of the Old Testament Scriptures Timothy had known from childhood. And 2 Peter 3:16 speaks of Paul's letters in the same breath as “the rest of the Scriptures”, which shows that within the New Testament period apostolic writings were already being read alongside the Law and the Prophets.

From these and similar texts the church has confessed that the Bible is the word of God given through human writers, fully divine in its origin and fully human in its language, style, and circumstances, and that it is the authoritative witness to God's self-revelation in Israel and above all in Jesus Christ. How that confession is spelled out differs. Many evangelical Protestants hold that Scripture is without error in all that it affirms, as set out in the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy of 1978; others in the same tradition prefer to speak of Scripture's infallibility in matters of faith and practice. The Catholic Church teaches, in the Second Vatican Council's constitution Dei Verbum (1965), that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wished to be recorded for the sake of salvation, and that it is read within the church's living tradition. Orthodox Christians read Scripture as the heart of holy tradition. Mainline Protestant churches generally affirm Scripture's unique authority while giving more room to historical criticism of its human elements. What these traditions share is more basic than what divides them: the Bible is not a book about human religious experience that happens to mention God, but the place where God has spoken and still speaks.

Beneath the variety of the library runs a single story, and learning its outline is the most useful thing a new reader can do. It begins with creation: one God makes a good world and sets human beings in it as his image, to rule it on his behalf (Genesis 1 and 2). It turns quickly to rebellion and its consequences, as the first humans reach for knowledge on their own terms, and violence and death spread through the human family (Genesis 3 to 11).

God's answer is a promise to one man, Abraham, around the early second millennium BC: through his family all the families of the earth will be blessed (Genesis 12:1-3). Abraham's descendants go down into Egypt, are enslaved, and are rescued in the exodus, the Bible's great act of deliverance; at Mount Sinai God binds Israel to himself by covenant and gives them the law and the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary where he dwells among them. Israel enters the land of Canaan, is ruled by judges, and then by kings; David, around 1000 BC, receives the promise that his house and throne will last forever (2 Samuel 7). The kingdom divides after Solomon, the prophets warn, and both kingdoms fall: Israel to Assyria in 722 BC, Judah to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC, when the temple is destroyed and the people go into exile. Under Persia, from 539/538 BC, some return and rebuild, but the prophets' larger promises of a new covenant, a new heart, and a coming king remain open.

The New Testament claims that those promises are kept in Jesus of Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate around AD 30 or 33 and raised from the dead on the third day. He is the son of David, the servant of the LORD, and the one in whom God himself comes to his people. The Holy Spirit is poured out, and the good news goes from Jerusalem to the nations, forming a new people of Jews and Gentiles together. The story ends not with souls escaping the world but with the renewal of creation: a new heaven and a new earth, where God dwells with his people and death is no more (Revelation 21 and 22).

The Study Bible's story path walks the whole Bible along this line, chapter by chapter, and every chapter note says where that chapter stands in it.

The Bible was not written to be read straight through from Genesis to Revelation on a first attempt, and many who try stall somewhere in Leviticus. A better way is to start where the story is clearest and then widen out. The Gospel of Mark is short, fast, and vivid, and can be read in an evening; Luke is fuller and more carefully ordered, and its sequel, Acts, carries the story on. Genesis gives the beginning of everything and the stories of the patriarchs. The Psalms show how Israel prayed in joy, grief, anger, and trust, and have been the prayer book of Jews and Christians for more than two thousand years. After these, Exodus, 1 and 2 Samuel, Isaiah, John, and Romans open the rest of the library.

Three habits help. Read whole units rather than single verses: a story, a psalm, a letter in one sitting when possible, since the chapter and verse numbers were added more than a thousand years after the books were written. Ask what kind of writing you are reading and what it meant to its first hearers before asking what it means now. And read with others, since the Bible was written for communities, read aloud in assemblies (1 Thessalonians 5:27 asks that Paul's letter be read to all the believers), and has always been best understood in company. The Ethiopian official in Acts 8 is reading Isaiah on the road when Philip asks if he understands it, and he answers that he cannot, “unless someone guides me” (Acts 8:31). That is not a confession of failure but the ordinary way into a large and ancient book.
